It was once well said of a certain German book that it does not permit itself to be read, and in the same way there are some secrets which do not permit themselves to be told. <break time="0.8s" /> Many a man dies quietly in his bed with a secret still locked in his heart, unable to reveal the very mystery that has haunted his conscience for years. <break time="0.8s" /> Not long ago, one autumn evening, I sat at the large bow window of a coffee house in London, for I had been ill for several months and was only now recovering my strength. <break time="0.8s" /> Freed at last from the dull fog of illness, I was in one of those rare moods of heightened keenness, when the film seems to fall from the minds eye and every trifle offers calm delight. <break time="0.8s" /> For some time I amused myself by reading the advertisements in a newspaper, but at length my attention was drawn to the street outside, which was one of the principal thoroughfares of the city. <break time="0.8s" /> As darkness came on, the throng thickened every moment, and by the time the lamps were lit, two dense and continuous tides of people were rushing past the door. <break time="0.8s" /> I had never before been in a similar situation at such an hour, and the tumultuous sea of human heads filled me with a delicious novelty of emotion. <break time="0.8s" /> At first my observations took an abstract and general turn, but soon I descended to details, regarding with minute interest the innumerable varieties of figure, dress, air, gait, and expression.

By far the larger part of the passers by wore a contented, business like look, as if their only thought were to make their way through the press of bodies. <break time="0.8s" /> Others, still a numerous class, moved restlessly and muttered to themselves, and if anyone jostled them, they bowed deeply to the offender as though overwhelmed with confusion. <break time="0.8s" /> There were clerks of every rank, the junior ones in tight coats and bright boots, the senior ones with slightly bald heads and right ears long accustomed to holding a pen. <break time="0.8s" /> Then came a race of well dressed pickpockets and gamblers, whose fine clothes and quick, watchful eyes betrayed the very trade they took such pains to conceal from the honest crowd. <break time="0.8s" /> Descending lower in the scale of humanity, I saw pale beggars, feeble invalids, and modest young girls returning from long labor, who shrank from the rude glances of passing ruffians. <break time="0.8s" /> There were also countless drunkards, some in rags and staggering, others still in decent clothes but with faces already marked by the slow ruin of drink and despair. <break time="0.8s" /> As the night deepened, the gas lamps, which at first had struggled feebly with the dying day, had at last gained the upper hand and threw over everything a fitful and garish luster. <break time="0.8s" /> With my brow pressed to the glass, I studied the faces one by one, and although the swiftness with which they passed allowed me only a glance, I seemed to read in each the history of long years.

Suddenly there came into view a decrepit old man of some sixty five or seventy years, whose countenance at once arrested and absorbed my whole attention, on account of its absolute strangeness. <break time="0.8s" /> Never before had I seen anything even remotely resembling that expression, and as I tried to analyze it, a crowd of contradictory ideas arose confusedly in my mind. <break time="0.8s" /> Ideas of vast mental power, of caution and avarice, of coolness and malice, of triumph and merriment, of excessive terror, and of intense, supreme despair all seemed written upon that single face. <break time="0.8s" /> How wild a history, I said to myself, is written within that bosom, and I felt a craving desire to keep the man in view, to know more of him. <break time="0.8s" /> Hurriedly putting on my overcoat and seizing my hat and cane, I made my way into the street and pushed through the crowd in the direction he had taken, for he had already disappeared. <break time="0.8s" /> With some little difficulty I at length came within sight of him, and I followed closely yet cautiously, so as not to attract the attention of this strange and restless figure. <break time="0.8s" /> He was short in stature, very thin, and apparently very feeble, and his clothes were filthy and ragged, yet the linen he wore, though dirty, was of beautiful texture. <break time="0.8s" /> Through a rent in his closely buttoned cloak, I caught a glimpse both of a diamond and of a dagger, a discovery which only heightened my curiosity and made me resolve to follow him wherever he went.
